Golden tanager (Tangara arthus) nestlings emerge from eggs incubated for approximately 12 days [ab = approximately 12 days] when the ambient temperature around the nest is 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a thermal regime typical of its mid-elevation cloud forest habitat. At hatching, these altricial chicks weigh a mere 2.86 grams [Ww0 = 2.86 grams], a modest initial mass that reflects the substantial yolk investment required for rapid post-hatching development. During the first days of life, the feather-growing nestlings are brooded intensively by both parents, who arrive frequently with arthropod prey to satisfy the growing chick's energetic demands. The progression of pin-feather eruption and body mass gain is remarkably swift, allowing the developing chick to achieve thermal independence well before fledging. By the time the nestling bird's primary flight feathers have reached functional length, the individual has undergone a dramatic transformation from a nearly naked hatchling to a fully feathered juvenile capable of short flights around the nest vicinity.

Within the context of active thermoregulation at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], resting metabolic rate measurements for adult Tangara arthus have recorded a basal oxygen consumption of 67.27 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 67.27 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value consistent with its body size among Neotropical tanagers. This metabolic datum was obtained from respirometry trials conducted on post-absorptive adults during their natural rest phase, ensuring the measurement reflects true basal conditions. The elevated body temperature of 41.6 °C is characteristic of passerine birds and underpins their high aerobic capacity for sustained foraging flights in the dense forest canopy. Comparative data from closely related Thraupidae species suggest that this metabolic rate is somewhat above the allometric prediction for a bird of that mass, perhaps reflecting the energetic demands of a frugivorous diet rich in simple sugars. Field metabolic rate studies would likely reveal considerably higher daily energy expenditures, especially during the breeding season when provisioning nestlings imposes substantial additional costs on both parents.

Females of this species attain an ultimate adult body mass of 23.1 grams [Wwi = 23.1 grams], representing the maximum recorded wet weight observed in reproductively active individuals during field surveys. This adult mass is roughly eight times the neonatal value, indicating a prolonged period of somatic growth before the onset of reproductive maturity. Under the thermal conditions typical of active individuals (41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]), sexual maturity, defined by the initiation of gonadal development, occurs at approximately 30 days after hatching [tp = approximately 30 days after hatching], a developmental milestone that precedes full structural growth. The delay between reaching puberty and engaging in actual breeding activities is considerable, as young birds must first acquire a territory and develop foraging proficiency. Immature individuals can often be identified by their duller plumage and less coordinated flight maneuvers, gradually acquiring the brilliant yellow-and-black adult coloration over several months. The ultimate body mass of 23.1 grams [Wwi = 23.1 grams] is a critical determinant of reproductive success, as heavier females tend to produce larger clutches and provision their broods more effectively.

Reproductive output in Tangara arthus follows a pattern typical of tropical passerines, with females laying clutches of 1 to 2 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 1 to 2 eggs per clutch] and producing approximately 1 clutch per year [F_R_i = approximately 1 clutch per year], a conservative strategy compared to temperate-zone relatives. Under the thermal conditions of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C] characteristic of active individuals, the first breeding event typically occurs at 0.98 years after hatching [tR = 0.98 years after hatching], suggesting that once a bird reaches adult mass, reproductive competence follows quickly. This single annual clutch is likely an adaptation to the relatively stable but resource-limited environment of cloud forests, where food availability fluctuates seasonally but rarely reaches the superabundant peaks seen in temperate ecosystems. The extended period of parental care, which includes both brooding and feeding of the altricial nestlings for several weeks, further constrains the number of broods a pair can successfully raise in a single season. Nest predation rates are also substantial, with many pairs experiencing at least one failed nesting attempt before successfully fledging young.

The maximum lifespan documented for this species in the wild is approximately 9.5 years [am = approximately 9.5 years] at a body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], derived from long-term banding studies in undisturbed Andean forest fragments. This longevity is notable among small passerines and likely reflects the low extrinsic mortality rates typical of tropical environments, where predation pressure is reduced compared to temperate systems. Fledging occurs at 10 days after hatching [tx = 10 days after hatching] under the same thermal regime of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], representing a relatively short nestling period for a bird of its body size. The post-fledging phase is a critical period of high mortality, as young birds must quickly learn to identify ripe fruits and evade predators while still receiving occasional food from their parents. Senescent individuals show reduced feather quality and lower reproductive output, with older females producing smaller clutches that fledge fewer young. The combination of a long lifespan, low annual reproductive output, and extended parental care places Tangara arthus firmly within the slow end of the life-history continuum among Neotropical passerines.

Recent studies on the foraging ecology of Tangara arthus have highlighted the importance of fruit availability in shaping its seasonal breeding patterns. During the peak fruiting period in the wet season, adult birds exhibit increased foraging activity and body mass maintenance. Observations of color-banded individuals in the Ecuadorian Andes confirm that juveniles disperse approximately 2 to 3 kilometers from natal territories, a behavior that promotes gene flow among fragmented populations. This dispersal strategy, combined with the species' reliance on a diverse array of fruiting plants, underscores its ecological role as a seed disperser in montane cloud forests. Ongoing habitat fragmentation poses a significant threat to these populations, as the removal of key fruit-bearing trees reduces the carrying capacity of remaining forest patches. Conservation efforts aimed at preserving connectivity between forest fragments are therefore critical for the long-term persistence of this species in its native Andean range.
